0x3e8.name: raise trap zero
0x3e8.why: the whole routine is `trap #$0`. Two bytes; nothing else to say about it.

0x620.name: lower the interrupt mask to zero
0x620.why: `move.w #$2000,sr; rts` - supervisor, trace off, mask 0. The counterpart of saveInterruptMaskRaise, which sets it the other way.

0x626.name: set interrupt mask from argument
0x626.why: move.w sr,d0 then move.w $6(a7),sr: it installs the status word the caller pushed and hands back the one it replaced, which is what makes it usable as a save-and-set pair with the caller's own restore.

0x62e.name: halt with every interrupt masked
0x62e.why: the whole routine is `stop #$2700` - halt, supervisor, interrupt mask 7. 0x642 is a second entry doing exactly the same thing.

0x632.name: raise trap zero unless d0 is set
0x632.why: `nop; nop; tst.w d0; bne $3ea; jmp $3e8` - falls through to the trap at 0x3e8 when d0 is zero and skips it otherwise. An assertion.

0x642.name: halt with every interrupt masked, second entry

0x646.name: two nops, then fall through
0x646.why: `nop; nop` with no terminator: a patch slot the routine after it runs into.

0x64a.name: save interrupt mask and raise it
0x64a.why: move.w sr,$3e0804 then move.w #$2500,sr - saves the status register to a fixed word and sets supervisor with interrupt level 5. 0x656 is the other half and reads the same word back.

0x656.name: restore saved interrupt mask
0x656.why: move.w $3e0804.l,sr and rts, the exact word 0x64a saved, and the two have the same six callers.

0x8b4.name: piece walker
0x8b4.why: walks a byte-encoded path over the board from a starting cell. a3 is the byte stream at $a(a6); each pair of bytes is added to the running x,y at 8(a6)/9(a6), which are then bounds-checked against $2a and $1e - the board is 42 by 30 cells. 0xfcca gives the cell-address delta per direction and 0xfcda/0xfce2 the x and y deltas, and a 0x0b byte in the stream switches to a second step. The 0xc0 mask on the cell byte is the owner field, compared against the current player's byte from 0x1000a indexed by the player at 0x3e1960+2; when $e(a6) is non-zero it stamps the cell and calls the sprite draw at 0x2338. A negative byte ends the walk.

0xbc2.name: enclosure test
0xbc2.why: walks the boundary of a wall from the cell at 8(a6) in the direction at $e(a6), turning left or right by whether the cell ahead carries the current player's wall byte - 0x1000a indexed by the player at 0x3e1960+2, or'd with 1 and with 3 for the two wall forms - and counting the turns in the word at -2(a6). It stops when the walk returns to the cell it started from (cmpa.l d3,a4) and answers whether the net turn count is -4: four turns the same way round a closed rectilinear loop is a winding number of one, which is an enclosure.

0xcac.name: walk the eight neighbours of a cell for the current player's wall
0xcac.why: 0xFCCA is the eight-way step table this ROM uses everywhere; this takes the current player's owner byte through 0x1000A, ors in 1 for a wall, and walks the neighbours of the cell cellAddress returns, with 0xFCEA as a second table for the diagonal cases.

0x10de.name: draw the cell in whichever way its type and owner call for
0x10de.why: a jump table's worth of tails: the owner nibble at -0xD(a6) shifted right six selects a wall byte from 0x1000E and writes it through cellWriteHelper with 8; other entries call cellDraw, cellOverlayDrawSecondForm or cellStateDraw on the same cell word at -0x14(a6), or clear the top two bits of the byte at -4(a6). Every path ends at 0x11EA or 0x11DE.

0x11c6.name: call the player's handler, then clear the top two bits of its byte
0x11c6.why: pushes the frame's pointer at -0x12 and the word the pointer at -0xC names, calls through the handler at -8, and on a non-zero d2 does `andi.b #$3f,(a0)` on the byte at -4 - the owner bits cleared, the rest kept.

0x122c.name: scan the whole board for cells of type one and their neighbours
0x122c.why: walks the board from 0x3E0864, masking each cell with 0x3F and looking for type 1, and for each looks at the eight neighbours through the step table at 0xFCCA. Two frame bytes at -1 and -2 carry the row and the answer.

0x13b2.name: walk the eight neighbours of a cell in screen space as well as board space
0x13b2.why: takes both cellAddress and screenAddress for the same coordinate, works out the parity of the two coordinate bytes, keeps the cell's owner bits with `andi.w #$c0`, and walks the 0xFCCA steps four at a time.

0x15b4.name: set flag after player array
0x15b4.why: writes 0xff to 0x3e1ae2, which is 0x3e1968 + 3 * 0x7e - the byte immediately after the third player's struct, in an array whose stride 0x7e and count of three are what 0x15d6 next door loops over.

0x15d6.name: clear status bits in every player
0x15d6.why: lea 0x3e1968, and.w #$6bff,(a0), lea $7e(a0),a0, three times: it clears bits 15, 12 and 10 of the flag word at offset 0 of each of the three player structs. The 0x7e stride and the count of three are the player array.

0x15fe.name: open the round: clear the hand slots and seed the protection counter
0x15fe.why: writes 0xFF into the three bytes at 0x3E0DCE - the hand slots - and, once 0x3E1952 has passed 1, copies 0x3E0DD4 into 0x3E0DD2 and seeds 0x3E0DE6 from the table at 0xFD06 indexed one past it. Then testWordProtectionWindow and the rest of the round's setup.

0x18a6.name: point each active player at its script, counting sign bytes
0x18a6.why: clears 0x3E0DD8, then for each of the three players whose first word has either owner bit set: indexes the pointer table at +0x16 of the block at 0x3E0DCA by the player's byte at +3, and walks that pointer forward two bytes at a time, skipping runs of non-negative bytes, once for each of the count in the player's byte at 0x1D. The address it lands on goes in field 0x4A.

0x1b96.name: count the round up for every player still in, and reset their state
0x1b96.why: for each of the three player structs with bit 11 set: counts the byte at +0x1E, raises 0x3E186D to a maximum of 2, clears the long at +0x28 and the byte at +0x16, runs playerFlagHandler, and walks the list at +0x6A. 0x3E1954 and 0x3E1956 are the flags it consults.

0x1c66.name: count the players still in and pick who acts next
0x1c66.why: walks the three player structs, counting those with bit 15 set and a non-zero byte at +0x14, and keeps the running answers in the frame - the count at -6, the chosen index at -2 starting from 0xFF, and 0x3E1952's value at -0xC. 0x3E1954 is the mode flag.

0x1e74.name: advance to the next active player, or wrap to the first
0x1e74.why: `seq` on the caller's word decides whether to look at the byte at +0x1E; then it walks the three structs for one with bit 15 set, keeping 0x3E195C and 0x3E1952 up to date. The counterpart of 0x1C66, which counts rather than advances.

0x1f3a.name: raise player counter capped at four
0x1f3a.why: multiplies the word argument at 6(a7) by 126 - add.l d0,d0 then asl.l #6 then subtract, which is x2 then x128 minus x2 - and 126 is 0x7e, the player stride, so it indexes the player array at 0x3e1968. It then increments the byte at 0x1d of that player unless it has already reached 4, the cmpi.b #$4 / bcc skipping the addq.

0x1f82.name: retire the entity: redraw it, release its hand slot and clear its flags
0x1f82.why: with a non-zero flag it calls entityDrawDispatch on the record and handTableEntryTwelvePast with the byte at +2. Either way it clears all but 0x71FF of the record's first word, writes 0xFF into the byte at 0x3E0DCE indexed by the record's byte at +3, and clears field 0x1D when 0x3E1954 is exactly 1.

0x219a.name: read the DIP switches and split them into the option bytes
0x219a.why: reads sound request 0x15 into 0x3E0DE0; bit 13 set means the word at 0x284 replaces it and is sent back. Then the low two bits go to 0x3E0DDA and bits 2 and 3 are masked off for the next option.

0x220c.name: entity spawn
0x220c.why: pushes two zero longs, then the three word arguments at $a/$e/$12(a7) sign-extended, then the longword from the table at 0xfd5e indexed by the byte at $2b(a7) times four - a descriptor pointer per kind - and calls the allocator at 0x5b40. So it is the by-kind spawn: kind byte in, descriptor and three coordinates out to the allocator.

0x2788.name: dispatch a cell type between 0x1A and 0x29 through its table
0x2788.why: `moveq #$1a,d1; cmp.l d0,d1; bgt` and `moveq #$29,d1; ...; blt` bound the index, then `jmp $27a2(pc,d0.w)` through the word table at 0x276E. What capstone shows after the jump is that table, not code.

0x3242.name: redraw a cell and the sprite that sits on it
0x3242.why: cellDrawCoordinate for the sprite, cellAddress for the cell, and the cell's owner nibble shifted right six indexes 0xFE06 for the tile. Counts the caller's byte at 0x19(a7) down, then screenAddress.

0x357a.name: walk a rectangle of cells calling a supplied routine for each
0x357a.why: the only indirect call in it is `jsr (a3)` where a3 came from the caller, so this is a higher-order walk rather than a blit of its own: for each of height rows and width columns it takes the next WORD from the source list and calls the supplied routine with that word, the running address, and a constant the caller passed - then takes the routine's answer as the new running address. Between rows it adds ((0x40 - width) << 3) + 0xe00, which together with whatever the callee advanced per column is what steps to the next row, so the two have to agree about the per-cell stride and neither says what it is alone.

0x3c00.name: score a cell from both neighbour weightings and bias by 0xA0
0x3c00.why: calls scoreNeighboursOneStrideEither and translates its answer through the table at 0xFDAC, calls scoreThreeNeighboursWeightsOne and translates that through 0xFD9C, adds the two and 0xA0, and tail-jumps to 0x3CCC. Reached through a function-pointer table, so it is one scoring policy of several.

0x41be.name: draw the panel for a player, or nothing for a negative index
0x41be.why: a negative index returns immediately. Otherwise it multiplies the index by 0x7E to reach the player struct, indexes the block at 0x3E0DCA by the struct's byte at +3, and draws from there.

0x4332.name: draw one decompressed graphic at a screen row
0x4332.why: `jsr $11bec` - screenAddress - then conditionalDraw at 0x435A with 0xC0, and the result handed to decompressGraphicsAtDADDC. Three calls and the argument shuffling between them.

0x4552.name: fade the title screen's five palettes
0x4552.why: paletteFadeStep on banks 4 and 7 with tables 0x1EE60 and 0x1F1A0, then paletteFadeStepFlag on 0x1EFC0 and 0x1EC00, and paletteSequenceTables between them. Table addresses and bank numbers throughout.

0x463c.name: fade all seven palette banks a step
0x463c.why: paletteFadeStep seven times through a2, with tables 0x1ED20, 0x1ED40, 0x1ED60, 0x1ED80, 0x1EDA0, 0x1EEA0 and 0x1EF00 for banks 9 to 0xF. The table addresses and bank numbers are the whole routine.

0x4880.name: copy the four difficulty bytes out of 0xFE03 and run 0x48AE
0x4880.why: four `move.b` from 0xFE03, 0xFE07, 0xFE05 and 0xFE09 into 0x3E1CA6 to 0x3E1CA9, then one call. A fixed table read into a fixed block.

0x48ae.name: fade the two attract palettes according to the difficulty byte
0x48ae.why: in attract - 0x3E1954 exactly 1 - it takes the record at 0x3E1964 and sets a flag from whether its byte at +0x1D has reached 3, then works from table 0x1F240 with the high nibble of the difficulty byte at 0x3E1CA6, calling paletteFadeStep and paletteFadeStepFlag through a2 and a3.

0x4ab8.name: run the palette sequence for table 0x1EDA0 and start the level intro
0x4ab8.why: paletteFadeStep with 0x1EDA0 and 0xD, then 0xC724 with 0x1F540 and six more constants, then 0xC832 with 0xFFFC and three more, then levelIntroSequence. Four calls whose arguments are all immediates, so the table addresses are the whole of what distinguishes it.

0x4b0a.name: load the eight level palettes and start their fades
0x4b0a.why: waits a frame, then for each of eight word entries of the table at 0x1F7C0 calls helperPaletteUpdate into consecutive longs from 0x3C0360, and follows with two calls to the backwards-counting scheduler on bank 0xD with -0xC and -8.

0x4d44.name: run the palette sequence for table 0xFE18
0x4d44.why: seven pushed constants - 0, 8, 0xFE18, 0xD, 4, 3, 4 - and one call to 0xC688. The table address is what makes this entry different from its siblings; everything else is the same call.

0x4e20.name: fade bank eight to the level's palette, or to the attract one
0x4e20.why: with 0x3E1954 exactly 1 it picks the 0x20-byte entry of 0x1EE00 indexed by 0x3E195A plus one and uses steps 5, 5, 3; otherwise the fixed table 0x1F6B0 with 3, 5, 3. Either way 0xC832 then paletteFadeStep, both on bank 8.

0x5000.name: fade all three palette banks a step
0x5000.why: three `jsr $450c.w` - paletteFadeStep - with the same pointer and bank numbers 0, 1 and 2, then drops the pushed arguments. Reached through a function-pointer table, so it is one phase's palette handler.

0x5056.name: fill the six-entry list for a kind with freshly spawned entities
0x5056.why: does nothing if the list at 0xFE3E indexed by the kind already has a first entry. Otherwise spawns six entities, each stamped with the shape from 0x1F7F0 and bit 5 of its byte at +2, addressed as 0x10-byte records from 0x3E02D8, and links them into the list. The kind byte comes from 0xFD92.

0x5192.name: choose the cursor's shape from what the current record holds
0x5192.why: with no long at +0x24 of the block at 0x3E1960 it uses shape 0x1F7F2; otherwise it follows that pointer and, on finding a 0x46 there, picks the shape by the block's byte at +0x15. The sprite record is at +0x42.

0x52e2.name: move the cursor sprite to the current player's cell and flag it changed
0x52e2.why: takes the sprite record at +0x42 of the block at 0x3E1960, sets its words at +8 and +6 to `(byte << 3) + 8` of the two coordinate bytes at +0x48, and when the shape from 0x1FAFE differs from the one already in the record writes it and sets bit 5 of the byte at +2.

0x54a8.name: spawn the round's banner sprite and point 0x3E0EC2 at it
0x54a8.why: entitySpawn with 0xAE, 0x4D and 6, addressed as a 0x10-byte record from 0x3E02D8, its address kept in 0x3E0EC2. Then shape 0x1FB5C, bit 5 of the byte at +2, and the bank chosen by 0x3E1AE2.

0x5558.name: claim the pending flag, count the request and clear the slot's word
0x5558.why: `tst.b (a3)` leaves through 0x5578 when the flag is already set; otherwise counts 0x3E0DC4 up, clears the word the pointer at $62(a1) names, writes 0xFF into the flag, and calls through a2 with 0x48.

0x5572.name: drop four bytes of stack, then restore a2 and a3 and return
0x5572.why: `addq.l #$4,a7; bra.w $561c`, where 0x561C is the shared `movem.l (a7)+,a2-a3; rts` epilogue.

0x5578.name: count one off the byte a3 points at, then restore a2 and a3 and return
0x5578.why: `subq.b #$1,(a3); bra.w $561c` - one decrement and the shared epilogue.

0x557e.name: hold the attract text until it scrolls off, then start the next
0x557e.why: the word the pointer at $62(a1) names is the position: above 0x50 or below -0x50 it calls through a2 with 0x5D, runs walkWholeListFlagRaised and bumps 0x3E0DC4. Inside that band it counts the byte at (a3) down, and on reaching zero starts attractTextSequence, calls a2 with 0x14, reloads the counter with 0xB4 and sets 0x3E0DC4 to 3.

0x55c4.name: slide the record down the screen, and tear it down past 0xA0
0x55c4.why: counts 0x3E0EC0 up and adds it to the word at +6 every frame, so the step grows; once that word reaches 0xA0 it removes event 0x11BC6, runs the palette fade, and calls through a2 three times with 0x49, 0x2C and 0x14 before leaving through the shared epilogue at 0x561C.

0x561c.name: restore a2 and a3, then return
0x561c.why: `movem.l (a7)+,a2-a3; rts` - the epilogue half of a save/restore pair, reached as its own address so several exits can share it.

0x5818.name: draw the score panel's box and rule it into rows
0x5818.why: rectGrab for the box at 0x80, 0x59, 0x50, 0x38, then rules rows from 0x200004 with a pitch of 0xA8 and a spacing of `0xA00 / 0x40`, sixteen of them, 0x75 wide.

0x5892.name: rect grab
0x5892.why: a0 = 0x200004 + y * 0x200 + x, a1 = 0x21e000, then width bytes copied per row for height rows with the source advanced by 0x200 - width between them. 0x200 is the playfield row stride and 0x200004 its base, so it lifts a rectangle of the screen into the buffer at 0x21e000.

0x59ee.name: piece bag builder
0x59ee.why: the first word argument picks one of three bags - table 0xffc8 with its pointer at 0x3e1f0a, 0xffe0 at 0x3e1f0e, or 0xfff8 at 0x3e1f12 - and the second is the level, clamped to 4 by cmpi.w #$4/bls. The table entry is a run-length list: each byte says how many copies of the current piece index to emit, the index rises with each byte, and a negative byte ends it. d4 counts what was emitted, 0xff terminates the bag, and the two calls to 0x5ab0 four times over shuffle it through the scratch at 0x3e1ee0.

0x5afc.name: piece rotation
0x5afc.why: takes a pointer to a cursor, steps it on by four and looks at what it now points at: a non-zero long means there is another rotation and it answers 0, a zero long means the list ended so it steps on once more, writes the long there back into the cursor - the head of the ring - and answers 1. So the answer is 'did it wrap', which is what a rotation cycle needs to know.

0x5b40.name: entity allocator
0x5b40.why: refuses with -1 when the count at 0x3e02ca has reached 0x45, then raises the interrupt mask and takes the index at 0x3e02c6. That index addresses two parallel arrays at once: 0x3e0000 with a stride of 8 (asl.l #3) and 0x3e02d8 with a stride of 16 (asl.l #4), which is the same base and stride 0x5c80 walks 0x45 times. It fills the second from the descriptor the caller passed, resolves two pointers through 0xf2ee, packs the coordinates into 0x4(a4) and 0x6(a4) with the asl #7 that puts the sub-cell part in the low seven bits, links the entry with 0xf306, drops the mask and answers the index.

0x5c80.name: set flag bit 4 on every motion object
0x5c80.why: lea 0x3e02d8, dbra from 0x45, adda 0x10 each time: 70 entries of 16 bytes at the base the allocator at 0x5b40 hands out, with the same cap. Inside the loop it raises the interrupt mask, sets bit 4 of the byte at offset 2 if it is not already set, and drops the mask again - one entry at a time rather than once around the whole array.

0x5cce.name: reset the display list and its counters for a new round
0x5cce.why: saves the interrupt mask with 0x56, clears the word pairs at 0x3E02CA and 0x3E02CC, sets 0x3E02C6 to 1 and 0x3E02C8 to 0x47, clears 0x3E02B0 and 0x3E02B2, and then zeroes the three words at the head of work RAM.

0x5e38.name: seal event post
0x5e38.why: turns the cell address it is given into a coordinate pair by subtracting the board base 0x3e0864 and splitting the remainder - asr.l #5 for the row, andi.b #$1f for the column, so the board is 32 bytes to a row - and pushes those two bytes onto the coordinate stack that 0x663c hands out slots in. Around that it saves the current player's 0x66 field into 0x3e209c and puts it back afterwards, clears 0x58, sets 0x3c to 0xff, and calls 0xee90 with 0x11ae2. The player comes from the pointer at 0x3e1960.

0x5ea2.name: territory fill
0x5ea2.why: the scanline flood fill. It takes the current player's cell byte from 0x1000a indexed by the player's byte at offset 2, pops a coordinate, and stops when it pops 0xff - the stack's empty marker - pushing the marker back and scoring through 0x865e when 0x3c of the player is positive. Otherwise 0x11bd8 turns the coordinate into a cell address, cells whose 0xc0 owner bits already match are skipped, and 0x5fa6 and 0x62a6 find the two ends of the span. It then lays the player's wall byte or'd with 1 along the row above and the row below - the subq.b #$1 and addq.b #$2 on the y byte - by calling the span scanner at 0x65aa for each.

0x5fa6.name: lay the player's wall along the cell run, from table 0x11742
0x5fa6.why: 0x1000A maps a player index to its owner byte and 0x1000E to its wall byte; `ori.b #$1` on the owner is how this ROM spells 'a wall of that owner'. Takes the record's player index, its width from the word table 0x11742, both the cell and screen addresses of the coordinate, and works from the counter block at 0x3E1F16.

0x60be.name: charge the item, then decompress its graphic, writing the cell backwards
0x60be.why: findEntryMatchingWord on the frame's word, cellSignTest on the answer, accessorStateBlock, then deductItemSCost with 0x1C. It writes d4 into the cell at d5 and steps d5 *down*, then calls decompressOneEightPixelColumn with a width from the table a4 points at. 0x63CA is the same routine writing forwards.

0x6114.name: claim the cell for the player and redraw its neighbour if it is type two
0x6114.why: reads the byte one row and one column on - `d5 + 0x20 + 1` - into the frame, writes the owner bits into the cell at d5 with `andi.b #$3f; or.b d4`, and when that neighbour's low six bits are 2 passes it through the gate once - guarded by the byte at $14(a2) - and calls cellOwnerDraw with 1.

0x6166.name: claim the cell and pass it on when the neighbour is type 0x1A
0x6166.why: the same claim as 0x6114 - the byte a row and a column on read into the frame, the owner bits written into the cell at d5 - but the neighbour test is against 0x1A rather than 2, the guard byte at $14(a2) is stepped by two rather than one, and the redraw is framebufferPairDraw.

0x62a6.name: lay the player's wall along the next row, from the counter at 0x3E1F18
0x62a6.why: 0x1000A maps a player index to its owner byte and 0x1000E to its wall byte; `ori.b #$1` on the owner is how this ROM spells 'a wall of that owner'. The sibling of 0x5FA6, differing in the counter block it uses - 0x3E1F18 rather than 0x3E1F16 - and in stepping the caller's second coordinate byte by one before it starts.

0x63ca.name: charge the item, then decompress its graphic, writing the cell forwards
0x63ca.why: identical to 0x60BE - the same four calls with the same constants - except that it writes d5 into the cell at d4 and steps *up*, and leaves through 0x655E rather than 0x6252.

0x65aa.name: span scanner
0x65aa.why: walks from the cell at the first coordinate to the cell at the second, both turned into addresses by 0x11bd8, comparing each cell byte against the byte at 0xf(a6). It pushes a coordinate onto the stack at 0x663c at the START of each run that does not match, and steps past the rest of that run without pushing again - which is exactly the seed list a scanline fill needs from the row above or below the span it just filled.

0x66c8.name: scan the screen for cells, taking the value from the pointer
0x66c8.why: `move.b (a1),d4` then into tailFullScreenCellScan at 0x66D4. The byte a1 points at is the only thing this entry contributes.

0x66ce.name: scan the screen for cells with value six
0x66ce.why: `moveq #$6,d4` then into tailFullScreenCellScan at 0x66D4. The constant is the whole difference from 0x66C8.

0x670e.name: clear player pair and run script
0x670e.why: lea 0x3e1968 - the first player struct - clears the byte pair at 0x46 and 0x47, and calls the event post at 0xee90 with the script address 0x11ae8, a neighbour of the 0x11ae2 the seal post uses. Two bytes and a script, nothing else.

0x672e.name: move the cursor to the player's marked cell, unless event 0x11AE2 is up
0x672e.why: returns at once when eventTest finds 0x11AE2. Otherwise it takes the coordinate pair at +0x46 of the first player struct, calls cellAddress, and walks the players against the block at 0x3E1960.

0x67f6.name: redraw the record's whole wall run into the playfield
0x67f6.why: 0x1000A maps a player index to its owner byte and 0x1000E to its wall byte; `ori.b #$1` on the owner is how this ROM spells 'a wall of that owner'. Walks the board cells from 0x3E0864 and writes into the playfield from 0x200004, taking the tile shapes from the table at 0x21BE0 and toggling on the low bit of a counter, so alternate cells get alternate tiles.

0x6bc0.name: take the next free entry in the record's 0x1A-byte list and stamp it
0x6bc0.why: does nothing once the count at +0x16 has reached 0x1D. Otherwise it steps that count, walks the list at +0x6A for an entry whose byte at +1 is negative - reusing a dead one by clearing it - writes the caller's two bytes into it, sets +5 to 0xC, copies the owner byte from +2 of the record, sets +4 to 2, and returns the entry.

0x6c20.name: cannon aiming
0x6c20.why: steps one cannon of the player at 0x10(a7) towards where it should be pointing. a3 is the cursor at 0x6e(a2) into a list of 0x1a-byte entries whose head is 0x6a(a2); a negative first byte ends the list and resets the cursor to the head. For a live entry it turns the cannon's cell coordinates into pixels - times 8 - subtracts them from the target at 0x4e(a2) and 0x50(a2), and asks 0x11cf8 which of eight directions that is. If it differs from the direction byte at 0x4(a3) it moves ONE step towards it: (want - have) & 7 - 4 decides which way round is shorter, and the result is masked back to 7. Then it redraws through 0x2698 and advances the cursor by 0x1a.

0x6cae.name: fire trigger
0x6cae.why: fires the cannon at 0x72(a2). It refuses when 0x16(a3) is already set - a shot in flight - or when either cell coordinate byte is negative. The muzzle is the cannon's cell plus one, times eight, which is pixels; unless the byte at 0x3e1952 is 1 and the player at 0x3e1c84 is this one, the direction byte at 0x4(a3) then indexes the pair of tables at 0x11754 and 0x11764 by two for the per-direction x and y offsets. It spawns through 0x220c twice, nine and eight pixels up, takes the second entity's word from 0x1f920 through 0xf2fa, and stores the first entity - 0x3e02d8 indexed by the returned index times 16, the allocator's own array and stride - into 0x16(a3) as the shot in flight.

0x6ef8.name: which of the four neighbours of a cell are unowned
0x6ef8.why: checks the cells at +0x20 and -0x20 - one row either way - and the two beside them, adding 1, 2, 4 or 8 to the answer for each whose owner bits are clear. A four-bit mask of free directions.

0x6fb4.name: projectile scheduler
0x6fb4.why: advances the player's selected-cannon cursor at 0x72(a2) to the next cannon that can actually fire, trying at most four (dbra from 3) and wrapping to the list head at 0x6a(a2) whenever the entry's first byte goes negative. A cannon qualifies when its second byte is not negative and 0x16 - the shot in flight the fire trigger writes there - is zero; the first one that does gets the event at 0x11afa removed and the cursor stops on it. Same 0x1a stride and same head pointer as the aiming walk at 0x6c20.

0x7004.name: step every shot in flight and draw it
0x7004.why: walks the 0x1C-byte shot records from 0x3E0F48 through the pointer at +0x16, with accessorStateBlock and offsetRecordTableBase to hand and the four shape tables 0x1F8D8, 0x1F8EC, 0x1F900 and 0x1F910 chosen by what the shot is.

0x7008.name: projectile flight
0x7008.why: sits inside the routine at 0x7004 - facts.json has no extent for it because it is the movem of that routine's own prologue - and 0x7004 runs to 0x71b2. It flies a projectile along an arc: a2 is the record at 0x3e0f48 and a3 its display entry at 0x16(a2); the words at 0x6 and 0xa are added to the positions at 0x8 and 0xc, which are then shifted right by six into the entry's 0x8 and 0x6, so the low six bits are sub-pixel. The height at 0x10 is subtracted from the y before that shift and is itself advanced by the word at 0xe each tick, which is the fall; 0xe counts down and reaching zero is what ends the flight.

0x71c4.name: map cursor code 0x11 or 0x30 to its handler
0x71c4.why: `cmpi.w #$11,d1` jumps to 0x72EC, `cmpi.w #$30,d1` to 0x7318, and anything else to 0x735C. Two constants and a default; the routine is the table.

0x71dc.name: place the cursor sprite for a player, several ways
0x71dc.why: each entry multiplies the record's byte at +2 by 0x7E to reach that player's struct at 0x3E1968, calls through a4 with 0x128B0, and then some combination of 0x73DC and 0x6EF8 before writing the sprite's words: +8 from the byte at -0x18(a6) scaled by eight plus four, +6 from the byte at -0x17 scaled by eight. The entries differ in which of the two helpers they run and what they do with the answer.

0x73dc.name: walk the neighbours for a wall the record's owner does not hold
0x73dc.why: returns at once when the cell's owner bits already match the record's owner byte from 0x1000A; otherwise walks the 0xFCCA steps with a count of 3 and a stride of 1.

0x747a.name: stamp the wall byte for the cell's own owner
0x747a.why: cellAddress for the coordinate, the owner nibble shifted right six less one indexes 0x1000E for that owner's wall byte, and the cell is written with it.

0x74fa.name: dispatch the piece's low six bits through its thirty-seven-way table
0x74fa.why: `move.b (a0),d2; andi.b #$3f,d2` takes the low six bits of the byte the caller points at, rejects anything outside 1..0x25 to 0x7672, and jumps through the word table at 0x752C. a2 is pointed at 0x767C first, so every case has the same helper to hand.

0x7578.name: stamp the shot's cell, several ways by what it hit
0x7578.why: one entry writes type 0x27 for a 0x25 and type 3 otherwise, keeping the owner bits with `andi.b #$c0`, and redraws through 0x3242. Another calls through a2 with 8 and only proceeds on an answer of 8, then indexes by the cell's owner nibble shifted right six. Every entry leaves through 0x7670 or 0x7672.

0x767c.name: walk backwards along the run until the cell type changes
0x767c.why: compares each cell's low six bits against the caller's byte and steps back with `move.b -(a0),d2`, counting down the second coordinate byte in the frame, so it finds where a run of one type begins.

0x7800.name: aim the unit at the next cell of its path and step it
0x7800.why: translates the record's byte at +2 through the table at 0x1000A, asks 0x7870 for the coordinate pair - retrying with a zero flag when the first byte comes back negative - and on a valid pair copies it into the record's fields at +0x46 and calls unitStepWrapper.

0x7870.name: find the next cell of the path the unit can move to
0x7870.why: walks the board from 0x3E0864 a row at a time - `moveq #$20,d3` is the row stride - asking 0x7954 whether each candidate's wall run is unbroken, and keeps the answer in the frame at -6. 0x3E0F46 is the shot block it consults.

0x7954.name: is the cell's wall run unbroken in all eight directions
0x7954.why: starts from `seq` on whether the cell's byte equals the caller's, then for each of the eight steps in the table at 0xFCCA looks one cell out and two cells out: a matching neighbour whose own neighbour is a different non-empty owner clears the answer. Returns the flag.

0x7a24.name: phase countdown
0x7a24.why: counts down the byte at 0x3e1870. It first hands the current value and the word argument to 0x7a88, then decrements, and when the result goes negative removes the event 0x11b00 for that argument. While it is still positive and the argument is zero, a value of 5 or less indexes the table of longwords at 0x11792 by four and passes the entry to 0x90e6 - the gate that only forwards when the word at 0x3e1948 is set - so the last five ticks are the ones that announce themselves.

0x7b3e.name: draw each player's score line, wide or narrow
0x7b3e.why: textWidthMeasure with zero picks 2 or 0 as the base, and the strings come from 0x1178A. It then walks the three player structs from 0x3E1968 drawing one line each.

0x7c04.name: end the round: post the outcome event and set the follow-on state
0x7c04.why: posts the caller's event if there is one, forces 0x3E0DC4 to 0xFE, and for a non-negative outcome posts 0x11B1E, scans the entity list named by the long table at 0x117AE, and sets 0x3E0EBE to 1 or 2 depending on the outcome and on whether 0x3E195C has reached 2.

0x7cf0.name: draw the panel graphic for a slot, choosing the wide or narrow variant
0x7cf0.why: phase 0xD uses base 6 and colour 7, anything else base 0 and colour 0xB; textWidthMeasure with 1 adds three more to the base when it answers non-zero. The result indexes the long table at 0x21516 and goes to 0x41BE with 0xC.

0x7dce.name: draw the round summary screen
0x7dce.why: blits 0x35642 to 0x200004 at 0x2A by 0x1E through 0x36A2 with the palette at 0x3EF80, then walks the player structs drawing from the strings at 0x11784, and posts event 0x11BA2.

0x7ea4.name: move the score towards its target, at most 0x3D3 or 0xA1 a step
0x7ea4.why: takes the pair of longs at +4 and +0xC of the record - the shown value and what is left to add - clamps the step to 0x3D3, or to 0xA1 when what remains is smaller, adds it to one and subtracts it from the other. The score counting up on screen.

0x8008.name: post each active player's phase event, chosen by the difficulty byte
0x8008.why: walks the three player structs; for each with bit 15 set it takes the block at 0x3E0DCA, the difficulty bytes from 0xFE02, the shapes from 0x214FA, and posts one of 0x11BA8, 0x11BB4 or 0x11BBA through eventPost.

0x8326.name: redraw the cell one row below the record's position
0x8326.why: 0x1000A maps a player index to its owner byte and 0x1000E to its wall byte; `ori.b #$1` on the owner is how this ROM spells 'a wall of that owner'. Copies the record's coordinate pair from +0x30, adds one to the first byte, and takes both the cell and screen addresses of that.

0x84da.name: dissolve to the next screen when the record's bank has changed
0x84da.why: does nothing unless bit 12 of the record's first word is set and its byte at +2 differs from 0x3E1AE2. Then screenDissolve, runSequenceDifferentRoutineIndex, copySixteenWords for that bank, blits 0xAE034 to 0x200004, calls 0x54A8 and passes 0x13 through the gate.

0x8598.name: damage selector
0x8598.why: walks the three player structs at 0x3e1968 with the 0x7e stride, and for each one whose flag word has bit 15 set it picks a damage script: the table at 0x22 of the block pointed to by 0x3e0dca, indexed by the player's byte at offset 3 times four. It then steps that script forward by the player's counter at 0x1d - each step skipping words until a negative byte and then one more - stores the resulting pointer in 0x3e(a2), and posts 0x11bcc. 0x8606 is the handler that consumes 0x3e two bytes at a time.

0x8606.name: damage handler
0x8606.why: consumes the script pointer at 0x3e(a2) that 0x8598 set up. It reads the word there as a coordinate, turns it into a cell address with 0x11bd8, and when that cell is empty writes 0x30 into it and redraws through 0x3194 - which is the rubble. Either way it steps 0x3e on by two, and a negative byte at the new position ends the script and removes 0x11bcc, the event 0x8598 posted.

0x865e.name: territory scoring
0x865e.why: reads the territory count the fill accumulated in 0x58(a2) and walks the ten words at 0x117ce until one is not below it, which gives a band index; the parallel table of words at 0x117e2, indexed by that band times two, is the award, and it is added to 0x56(a2). It then calls 0x441c with the player and the band and sets 0x3c(a2) to 0xff, which is the byte 0x5ea2 tests before calling this at all.

0x875e.name: walk the current record's script to the terminating byte
0x875e.why: follows the pointer at +0x4A of the record at 0x3E1960 two bytes at a time, skipping over the caller's string while its bytes are non-zero, and reads the byte it lands on sign-extended.

0x88b0.name: sweep the five-by-five neighbourhood of a cell, freeing what it finds
0x88b0.why: steps both coordinate bytes back by one for a five-by-five box - the counts 4 and 4 in the frame - and runs runCellsFree at 0x8A24 on each, with 0xF and 0x30 as the masks.

0x8a9c.name: walk the path until it reaches the target cell, and say how far
0x8a9c.why: steps a coordinate pair by the deltas at 0xFCDA and 0xFCE2 indexed by each byte of the path, counting steps, and returns that count when the pair matches the caller's word. A negative path byte ends the walk and returns -1.

0x8b0c.name: step a path one cell and follow it from the current player's position
0x8b0c.why: adds the first two bytes of the path to the caller's coordinate pair, takes the current player's path pointer at +0x7A and coordinate pair at +0x30, and walks with the delta tables 0xFCDA and 0xFCE2.

0x8bb2.name: walk a record's whole path, cell by cell
0x8bb2.why: reads the record's path pointer at +0x7A for the starting pair and walks it with the same 0xFCDA and 0xFCE2 delta tables, calling cellAddress for each cell. The caller's word decides the direction with `sne`.

0x8c7a.name: follow the record's second path to its end
0x8c7a.why: takes the coordinate pair at +0x46 and the path pointer at +0x76 - the second of the record's two - and walks it with the 0xFCDA and 0xFCE2 delta tables until a negative byte ends it.

0x8d0e.name: retire the current record's path, and start the next stage
0x8d0e.why: with a long at +0x24 of the block at 0x3E1960: a byte of 0xFE at +0x22 clears bit 13 of the first word, walks the path with 0x8BB2 and writes 0xFD; the other cases carry the walk on with the 0xFCE2 deltas.

0x91b2.name: the main loop
0x91b2.why: initialisation once - the sound sequence player, the high score renderer, initialisePlayerStructs, entitySpawn, state word cleared and sub-state set to 1, the palette cleared, flagTestWord, difficultyClamp - and then an endless `bra.b` round drainEventQueueWrapper, runHandlerEveryFlagBit, the state dispatcher at 0x9208 and phaseDispatcher. This is the loop that never returns, which is why System.run does not either.

0x9208.name: dispatch the game state at 0x3E1948 through its twenty-four-way table
0x9208.why: `link a6,#-8`, points a4 at 0x3E1960 and a frame long at 0x3E194A, reads the state word at 0x3E1948, rejects anything above 0x17 to 0xA7DA, and jumps through the word table at 0x9236. The dispatcher the main game state machine sits under.

0x9d80.name: set the game state to 0xE, then to 0xC with a timer and two lines
0x9d80.why: `move.w #$e,$3e1948` and into 0x9E80; the second entry sets a phase timer of 0xF, draws a text line, calls 0xDEC8 with 1, and sets the state word to 0xC. Two entries into the same state change.

0x9db2.name: award the round to the current player and set up the next
0x9db2.why: with 0x3E1AE2 at 3 it just calls 0x1E74 with 1; otherwise it awards a thousand to that player, reads their field, raises their counter capped at four, and calls 0x1E74 with zero. Then roundTeardown, and either 0x3E1958 set to 3 in attract or a4 pointed back at the first player struct.

0x9e80.name: draw the state's message line and post its event
0x9e80.why: the entries share the state word at 0x3E1948 and the countdown byte at 0x3E1870: one leaves at once unless d5 is set and drains 0x11B3C; another draws a text line with the state number and the countdown as its arguments.

0xa000.name: point the handler slot at the player block and post event 0x11B7E
0xa000.why: `move.l $3e1964.l,(a4)` then `jsr $ee90.l` - eventPost - with 0x11B7E and a zero. Reached through a function-pointer table, so this is one phase's entry.

0xa016.name: the game's phase entries, one per state word
0xa016.why: each entry sets 0x3E1948 to the next state and leaves through 0xA7DA. Between them: waiting for event 0x11B06 to drain, resetting the players and the piece bag, arming the round with a countdown of 0xA at 0x3E1870, ending the round through 0x7C04 with event 0x11B24, and passing 0xE, 4 and 6 through the gate. This is the largest routine in the port at 1,162 bytes, and it is a switch, not a computation.

0xa4a0.name: the attract and join phases, one entry each
0xa4a0.why: the entries share the frame word at -4(a6) as their timer. One counts it down; one runs 0x7004 and unitMovement and only proceeds when both are quiet and the timer has expired; that one then, in attract, calls 0xC436 and reads and raises the counter for the player at 0x3E195A before reloading the timer with 0xB4. 0x3E1954, 0x3E1956 and 0x3E1CB4 are the flags they branch on.

0xa74a.name: drop twenty bytes of arguments and continue at 0xa7da
0xa74a.why: `lea $14(a7),a7; bra.w $a7da` - unwinds a caller's pushed arguments and tail-jumps. 0x14 is the argument block's size, not a frame.

0xa752.name: advance the operator menu, or run out its timer and start the game
0xa752.why: one entry steps the cursor by 0x7E - a player struct - and counts 0x3E1958. Another runs operatorMenu for 0x3E1954 less one and, when it answers non-zero, steps the same cursor, sets the frame word to 0x78 and the state to 0x15. A third counts that word down while event 0x11BA2 is absent and, at zero, clears the palette and runs the round summary.

0xa90e.name: hand the current record its table and post 0x11B48 for each player
0xa90e.why: points the record at 0x3E1C84's field +0x2C at 0x3E1C44, and in two player mode - 0x3E1954 exactly 2 - posts 0x11B48 for every player struct with bit 15 set, with that player's owner byte from 0x1000A.

0xa9be.name: drain the round's four events and clear the current record
0xa9be.why: only when 0x3E1956 is set: drains 0x11B48 through eventQueueAccess, then removes 0x11B66, 0x11B6C and 0x11B78, and clears fields of the record at 0x3E1C84.

0xaa86.name: post the round-start events, one set in attract and another in play
0xaa86.why: in attract - 0x3E1954 exactly 1 - it posts 0x11B72 with zero and 0x11B4E with the current record at 0x3E1C84; otherwise it walks the three player structs posting one each.

0xab58.name: point the message pointer at the string for the current option
0xab58.why: in attract it indexes the 0x1A-byte entries of 0x11842 by the option byte at 0x3E0DDA and stores the address in 0x3E1C9A, then reads the record at 0x3E1964's byte at +0x1D to choose within it.

0xad5a.name: split a cell number into its row and column and act on each
0xad5a.why: `andi.w #$3f` takes the column and the rest shifted right six less one is the row; a column of zero means the whole row. 0x3E1C9E is the block it works through.

0xaef2.name: pick a random one of the twenty entries and mark it
0xaef2.why: rng with 0xA, floored at 3, indexes the twenty 0x13-byte entries the pointer at +0x1E of the block at 0x3E0DCA names, and 0x1A goes in the frame byte. 0x3E1AE4 is the block it records into.

0xaf72.name: unit movement
0xaf72.why: walks seven units - lea 0x3e1bc6, adda 0x12, dbra from 6 - and moves each one that has a display entry at 0x4. The words at 0xe and 0x10 are the velocity and are added to the position at 0xa and 0xc; the position is then shifted right by five into 0x8 and 0x6 of the display entry, so the low five bits are sub-pixel, and bit 5 of the entry's byte 2 is set to mark it for redraw. The counter at 0x8 counts the move down and retires the unit through 0xb53a when it reaches zero. The answer is 1 if anything is still moving.

0xafda.name: expand one of three random score strings into the buffer
0xafda.why: rng with 3 picks between the strings at 0x1181A, 0x11820 and 0x11826, then copies each byte of it plus the caller's word, masked to three bits, into the destination until a negative byte ends it, and terminates with 0xFF.

0xb032.name: advance the current record to the next moving unit, wrapping
0xb032.why: adds 0xE to the record's pointer at +0x34 and wraps to 0x3E1AE6 when it reaches the end of the units at 0x3E1BC6, writing it back. cellWriteHelper and the string at 0x11808 are what it then draws with.

0xb330.name: is the cell part of a castle, and which corner
0xb330.why: cellAddress, then the cell must be type 5; the cell before it must be 5, 7 or 6, and the cell a row on is read too. A castle is a block of those types, so this identifies one and says where in it the cell sits.

0xb3b4.name: index the shape table at 0x1F930 by kind, flip and frame
0xb3b4.why: builds an offset from three things - 8 when the byte at +1 is set, 0x10 for kind 0x24 and 0x20 for kind 0x25, plus the caller's word - doubles it, and hands 0x1F930 plus that to offsetRecordTableBase.

0xb40a.name: link the two records together and place the sprite between them
0xb40a.why: writes each record's address into the other - +8 of one, offset zero of the other - then takes the coordinate pair at +0xC and scales the first byte by eight plus eight for the sprite's position.

0xb53a.name: unlink the record and take its string from 0x11812
0xb53a.why: clears the long at +4 of the head and at +8 of the record it names, takes the coordinate pair at +0xC, and indexes 0x11812 by the byte at +4 of the record the pointer at +4 names.

0xb738.name: find the moving unit nearest the record, skipping the current one
0xb738.why: the record's owner byte is zero when it is the current one at 0x3E1C84, and its own owner from 0x1000A otherwise. Then it walks the seven 0x12-byte units at 0x3E1BC6 against the record's pointer at +0x34, with 0x3E1AE6 and 0x3E1CB0 as the bounds.

0xb958.name: which of the seven moving units is within 0x180 of the point
0xb958.why: scales both coordinates by 32, then for each of the seven 0x12-byte units at 0x3E1BC6 with a live pointer at +4 checks both differences lie between -0x180 and 0x180. On a hit it runs 0xB9C8 on the unit and answers 2 or 1 by the result; 0 if none is near.

0xb9c8.name: age the unit, faster once the round counter has passed two
0xb9c8.why: steps the byte at +1 of the unit by one, and by the round counter at +0x1E of the record at 0x3E1964 less two on top of that once that counter is above 2 - so units decay faster in later rounds.

0xbb7c.name: allocate a two-byte slot, stamp the cell and record its coordinates
0xbb7c.why: findFreeTwoByteSlot first, and does nothing if there is none. Otherwise cellAddress for the cell, writes the byte from the table at 0x1000A indexed by the current record's field +2 plus the caller's owner code, calls cellStateDraw, copies the two coordinate bytes into the slot and counts 0x3E1C98 on by four.

0xbbd2.name: walk the current record's ring of targets and act on each
0xbbd2.why: steps the pointer at +0x2C of the record at 0x3E1C84 by two, wrapping back to 0x3E1C44 when it reaches 0x3E1C84 itself - a ring - and works through what it finds. At 1,406 bytes this is the second largest routine in the port.

0xc240.name: draw the entity at a cell, one step brighter
0xc240.why: findEntryMatchingWord for the cell, screenAddress for the position, and helperUsedSpriteEntityUpdate with 1 and 1; the caller's byte at 0x1B is stepped on the way through.

0xc436.name: how much of the claimed area is left to award
0xc436.why: takes the record at 0x3E1964's byte at +0x16, multiplies it by six with shifts and adds, and subtracts that from the running total at 0x3E1C98.

0xc688.name: schedule a palette effect of kind five
0xc688.why: kind 5 into 0xc(a2), and allocates a record through 0xc504, stamps its kind byte at 0xc, and links it into the circular timer list at 0x3e20a0 that 0x125da ticks - with 0x3e2498 set to 1 across the link and cleared after, which is that ticker's own pause byte used as a critical section. The record's 0x8 is a palette RAM address: 0x3c0000 + (bank * 16 + index) * 4, plus 0x400 when the page argument is non-zero, so an entry is four bytes and a page is 0x400 - which is the 0x101 entries at stride 4 the self-test failure report at 0x13134 writes. 0x10 and 0x16 both take the value, current and original; 0xd is the tick period and 0xe is set to 1 so it fires on the next tick; 0x14 and 0x15 are a second period and its remainder. Kind five stores the repeat count MINUS ONE at 0xf; kind four at 0xc724 is otherwise the same routine and stores it as it stands.

0xc724.name: schedule a palette effect of kind four
0xc724.why: kind 4 into 0xc(a2), and allocates a record through 0xc504, stamps its kind byte at 0xc, and links it into the circular timer list at 0x3e20a0 that 0x125da ticks - with 0x3e2498 set to 1 across the link and cleared after, which is that ticker's own pause byte used as a critical section. The record's 0x8 is a palette RAM address: 0x3c0000 + (bank * 16 + index) * 4, plus 0x400 when the page argument is non-zero, so an entry is four bytes and a page is 0x400 - which is the 0x101 entries at stride 4 the self-test failure report at 0x13134 writes. 0x10 and 0x16 both take the value, current and original; 0xd is the tick period and 0xe is set to 1 so it fires on the next tick; 0x14 and 0x15 are a second period and its remainder. Identical to 0xc688 instruction for instruction apart from the kind byte, a different register pair carrying the same arithmetic, and the repeat count: kind four stores it as it stands where kind five stores it minus one.

0xc7bc.name: schedule palette effect kind six over a whole bank
0xc7bc.why: takeFirstItemListZero hands back a free effect record or nothing; the record's byte at +0xC is the effect kind, +8 the palette address, +0x10 the table, and +0xE and +0xF the step and count. The bank's second half is selected by adding 0x200 words. Kind 6, addressing a whole bank with `bank << 5`, and it sets the step to 0x10 and the count to 1 and raises 0x3E2498.

0xc832.name: schedule a palette effect counting backwards from an entry
0xc832.why: takeFirstItemListZero hands back a free effect record or nothing; the record's byte at +0xC is the effect kind, +8 the palette address, +0x10 the table, and +0xE and +0xF the step and count. The bank's second half is selected by adding 0x200 words. The sign of the caller's byte picks the direction: negative counts down from `(bank << 4) + index` less that byte less one, non-negative counts up. The kind comes from the caller too, which is why this one is called with 0xD and 0xFFFC and 0xFFF8 rather than a fixed number.

0xc8de.name: schedule a palette effect of kind two
0xc8de.why: kind 2 at 0xc, with a value longword at 0x10, the period at 0xd, and the delay argument PLUS ONE at 0xe, so it waits one tick longer than it says; 0xf is 1. Allocated through 0xc504 and linked into the circular timer list at 0x3e20a0 with 0x3e2498 held set across the link, the same critical section 0xc688 and 0xc724 use. The palette address at 0x8 is 0x3c0000 + bank * 64 + page * 0x400 - the bank shifted left five and doubled, which is sixteen four-byte entries - so these two take a whole BANK where kinds four and five take a bank and an index within it.

0xc95e.name: schedule a palette effect of kind three
0xc95e.why: kind 3 at 0xc, the period at 0xd and the delay argument PLUS ONE at 0xe. It stores no value at all, where kind two next door does - which is the whole difference between them and the reason kind three takes one fewer argument. Allocated through 0xc504 and linked into the circular timer list at 0x3e20a0 with 0x3e2498 held set across the link, the same critical section 0xc688 and 0xc724 use. The palette address at 0x8 is 0x3c0000 + bank * 64 + page * 0x400 - the bank shifted left five and doubled, which is sixteen four-byte entries - so these two take a whole BANK where kinds four and five take a bank and an index within it.

0xcae2.name: scheduled trigger
0xcae2.why: three word arguments and three conditions, all of them equalities against fixed bytes: 0x3e195c must equal the third, 0x3e1870 - the phase countdown byte 0x7a24 decrements - must equal the first, and 0x3e1950 must be zero. Only then does it call 0xcbae with the second. Nothing else happens either way.

0xcb24.name: post 0x11B0C for each player not already carrying 0x11B06
0xcb24.why: for each of the three player structs, `pairAlreadyEventQueue` asks whether 0x11B06 is already queued for it, and only if not does it post 0x11B0C. 0xF is the count it works to.

0xcbae.name: dispatch each active player's pending action, five ways
0xcbae.why: walks the three player structs, skipping any whose first word lacks bit 15 or whose byte at 0x1D is set, and jumps through the five-way word table at 0xCC0E on the caller's selector. The two event ids 0x11924 and 0x11930 and the masks 0x3F and 0x40 are hoisted into registers for the cases to use.

0xcc18.name: pass the record's byte at 0x14 through the gate unless it is set
0xcc18.why: reads `$14(a3)` into the frame word at -2, and calls passByteOnlyWhenGate only when that word is zero; either way it leaves through 0xCC88.

0xcd4a.name: queue the entity for the record's script and stop the phase timer
0xcd4a.why: takes the two coordinate bytes at +0xC of the block at 0x3E0DCA indexed by the record's byte at +3, calls entitySpawnQueue with them, 2, 1 and the record's byte at +2 plus one, sets the record's byte at 0x1A to 2 and 0x3E1950 to 0x46, and calls phaseTimerStop.

0xcdae.name: format the caller's long against the string at 0x1FB10
0xcdae.why: `move.l $4(a7),d0; move.l d0,-(a7); pea $1fb10.l; bsr.b $cd4a; addq.l #$8,a7` - one argument and one fixed format string.

0xce76.name: total the sixteen-cell counts across the active players
0xce76.why: walks the three 0x7E-byte player structs, and for each with bit 15 set reads the byte at +0x16 and accumulates over 0x18 entries of 0x60. The constants 0x60, 0x18, 3 and 0x7E are hoisted before the loop.

0xcee8.name: post event 0x11BC0 for each player whose counter has passed 0x18
0xcee8.why: only once 0x3E1952 has reached 2. For each of the three 0x7E-byte player structs whose first word has bit 15 set and whose byte at +0x20 is above 0x18, it posts 0x11BC0 with the struct and writes 0xFF into the byte at +0x22.

0xcfda.name: dispatch the sub-state at 0x3E194C through its seventeen-way table
0xcfda.why: returns at once when the word at 0x3E194A is non-zero - the state machine is busy - then reads the byte at 0x3E194C, rejects anything outside 1..0x11, and jumps through the word table at 0xD00C.

0xd1ec.name: the round's phase sequence, one entry per phase
0xd1ec.why: each entry does a phase's work and sets the next phase byte at (a2) before falling into the shared tail: fade the palettes and give every player their own board (state 0xA); wait until events 0x11B1E, 0x11B8A and 0x11B90 have all drained, then clear the indices, walk the list, reset the palette sequence tables, clear the palette, clear a framebuffer band and set a 0x168 timer (state 0xB); or set a 0xB4 timer and test 0x11B00. The phase timer at (a3) and the phase byte at (a2) are the two things every entry touches.

0xd43a.name: run the battle phase's tick and decide which text line to draw
0xd43a.why: one entry sets the byte at (a2) to 1; the other counts the word at (a3) down and, at kind 4, runs 0x7004 and unitMovement, calling roundTeardown when the counter reaches zero. Then eventTest for 0x11B1E: present, it reads field six of the current record and draws line 0 if that is at least 0xA0 and line 1 otherwise; absent, line 1.

0xd490.name: reset the round: clear the queue, the hand slots and the block
0xd490.why: eventQueueReset first, then 0x3E195C set to 1, the three hand slots at 0x3E0DCE cleared and the block at 0x3E0DCA reindexed by the caller's word scaled by 0x18.

0xd6e6.name: take each active player's next target and post event 0x11B8A
0xd6e6.why: the sibling of 0xD74E: the same walk over the three player structs and the same per-player pointer at 0x3E1CB8 stepped by four, but the pair it reads goes into fields 0x32 and 0x33, the byte at 0x14 is copied to 0x15, the longs at 0x24 and 0x2C are set to 0xFFC4, and the event is 0x11B8A.

0xd74e.name: take each active player's next coordinate pair and post event 0x11B9C
0xd74e.why: walks the three 0x7E-byte player structs at 0x3E1968, and for each whose first word has bit 14 set steps that player's pointer at 0x3E1CB8 on by four, copies the two words it now names into fields 0x52 and 0x54, and posts 0x11B9C. Then chooseEachPlayerSStarting once at the end.

0xd854.name: make the record current, and remove its event unless the sub-state is 0xE
0xd854.why: writes the record into 0x3E1960, and unless 0x3E194C is 0xE draws the current piece and removes event 0x11AD0 for it.

0xdb04.name: checksum the five tables and start the cue the answer selects
0xdb04.why: reads sound request 0x16, and if it appears in the list at 0x1193C runs checksumTableAgainstStoredSum five times, oring each answer into 0x3E1CC8. A result of 0x22B starts cue 0x228 on channel 0x16; anything else keys channel 0x16 with 1.

0xdb6c.name: return the first stack argument
0xdb6c.why: `move.l $4(a7),d0; rts` - reads the longword above the return address and hands it back. 0xdb72 is a second, identical copy.

0xdb72.name: return the first stack argument, second copy
0xdb72.why: `move.l $4(a7),d0; rts`, byte for byte what 0xdb6c does, at its own address and separately called.

0xde1a.name: give each player a starting hand of three
0xde1a.why: for each player index it calls helperInitialisePlayerStructs with 3, masks the answer to two bits, and works through the countdown byte at 0x3E1870.

0xdec8.name: choose the player to act, by flag and by the caller's three words
0xdec8.why: walks the three player structs testing bit 15, keeping the best index in the frame at -4 starting from 0xFF, with the caller's three words as the criteria and 0x8000 and 1 hoisted into registers.

0xe0ee.name: draw the high score entry screen
0xe0ee.why: framebufferDraw's helper first, then blits the graphic the long at 0x214C6 names to 0x200004 at 0x2A by 0xA with the palette at 0x80, and draws the rest through drawParameterMarshaller at 0x35EE.

0xe5ae.name: seed the three players' starting positions from the random pick
0xe5ae.why: helperInitialisePlayerStructs with 3 gives an index masked to two bits, and the blocks at 0x3E1CD4 and 0x3E1CE0 hold the answers.

0xe7a8.name: is any player still in the game
0xe7a8.why: walks the three 0x7E-byte structs for the first with bit 15 set and answers with its index; four iterations, so it returns 3 when none is.

0xeaee.name: clear the six option bytes and reload them for the current mode
0xeaee.why: clears the six bytes at 0x3E1CEC, and when 0x3E195C is set indexes by 0x3E1CB4 scaled by four to reload them.

0xebba.name: drop sixteen bytes of arguments, then fall through
0xebba.why: `lea $10(a7),a7` and no terminator: unwinds the argument block and runs into the restore-and-return at 0xebbe.

0xebbe.name: restore d2 to d4 and a2 to a5, then return
0xebbe.why: `movem.l (a7)+,d2-d4/a2-a5; rts` - the epilogue for the routines that save that set, shared by address.

0xec3a.name: has the record reached its target, and what to do if not
0xec3a.why: compares the coordinate pair at +0x48 against the word at +0x32; equal means arrived. 0xECB0 - twoPlayerDrawGate - is held in a3 for the not-arrived path, and 0x3E1954 picks between one and two player rules.

0xed8e.name: draw the panel graphic for a slot at its fixed screen position
0xed8e.why: takes the difficulty byte at 0xFE02 indexed by the slot plus one, the screen address of the coordinate word from the table at 0x11AB4, and the graphic pointer from the long table at 0x215E6 indexed by the slot, and hands all of it to drawArgumentRepack with 0xC and 9.

0xee44.name: phase dispatcher
0xee44.why: the event list itself. The count is the word at 0x3e1cf4 and the entries start at 0x3e1cf6 with a stride of 0xc, which is the array 0xee90 appends to. Each tick it decrements the entry's word; when that reaches zero it reloads it from the byte at 2, checks the guard byte at 3 against 0x3e0802, and calls the routine whose pointer is at 4 with the longword at 8 as its argument.

0xee90.name: event post
0xee90.why: appends to the same array 0xee44 runs: count at 0x3e1cf4, entries at 0x3e1cf6 with a stride of 0xc. It first scans for an entry with the same routine pointer AND the same argument and does nothing if it finds one, so posting twice does not schedule twice. A new entry takes the routine from the descriptor's first long, the argument the caller passed, the period from the descriptor's byte 4 - written both as the reload at 2 and as the initial countdown at 0 - and the guard from byte 5.

0xeeee.name: event remove
0xeeee.why: the other end of 0xee90. Same array - count at 0x3e1cf4, entries at 0x3e1cf6 with a stride of 0xc - and the same match on routine pointer AND argument together. Having found one it compacts the array down over it, three longs per entry, writes 0x7fff into the countdown of the entry left at the end and clears its routine pointer so a stale one cannot fire, and decrements the count.

0xeffa.name: event test
0xeffa.why: the third operation on the event array 0xee90 appends to and 0xeeee compacts - count at 0x3e1cf4, entries at 0x3e1cf6, stride 0xc. It differs from the other two in what it matches on: the routine pointer ALONE, not the routine and the argument together, so it answers whether a routine is scheduled at all rather than whether one particular posting exists. Answers 1 or 0. The map splits it at 0xf000, so facts.json records this head as six bytes and the scan itself as the routine after it.

0xf630.name: rebuild the display list from the motion objects, highest priority first
0xf630.why: the display list at 0x3E02B4 is eight priority buckets of words, and 0x3E02D8 the 0x10-byte motion object records. `move.w #$2700,sr` masks every interrupt around the walk, because the frame handler reads the same list. This entry walks the eight buckets from 7 downwards, taking each record from 0x3E02D8 and threading it into the list at 0x3E0000.

0xf79e.name: rebuild the display list, skipping empty buckets
0xf79e.why: the display list at 0x3E02B4 is eight priority buckets of words, and 0x3E02D8 the 0x10-byte motion object records. `move.w #$2700,sr` masks every interrupt around the walk, because the frame handler reads the same list. The sibling of 0xF630: the same walk, but it reads the bucket word into d5 first and skips the bucket entirely when it is zero.

0xf936.name: rebuild the display list from the first bucket up
0xf936.why: the display list at 0x3E02B4 is eight priority buckets of words, and 0x3E02D8 the 0x10-byte motion object records. `move.w #$2700,sr` masks every interrupt around the walk, because the frame handler reads the same list. The third of the family, walking from bucket zero upward with a 0x10-byte record stride, and giving up as soon as 0x3E02B4 itself is empty.

0xfb80.name: checksum a table against its stored sum
0xfb80.why: checks one table per call and rotates through five of them: the byte at 0x3e1cca is stepped and wrapped at 5, and multiplied by 0xc to index 0x11e7e, where each entry is a start pointer, an end pointer and the expected sum. It adds longwords from start until the pointer reaches end, compares the total with the third field, and answers 1 on a mismatch and 0 on agreement.

0xfc1e.name: is the protection counter in step with 0x3E0DE6
0xfc1e.why: `move.b $3e0de6,d1; move.b $3e0de2,d0; eor.w d0,d1; btst.b #$0,d1` - the low bit of the exclusive or, so it asks whether the two counters agree in parity. Falls into the reader that steps the counter when they do not.

0xfc32.name: read the first protection word, then step the two-bit counter
0xfc32.why: `tst.w $1460bc` - a read of the board ROM window, which is what the protection check is - then `addq.w #$1,d0` and into stepTwoBitCounterToward at 0xFC3A. 0xFC88 is the same with 0x1461BC.

0xfc3a.name: keep the low two bits of the counter and store it
0xfc3a.why: `andi.w #$3,d0; move.b d0,$3e0de2` - the tail both protection-window readers at 0xFC32 and 0xFC88 fall into, which is why the counter at 0x3E0DE2 only ever holds 0 to 3.

0xfc74.name: the attract mode's copy of the protection parity check
0xfc74.why: byte for byte the same test as 0xFC1E on the same two counters, at its own address and called from attractModeController, falling into its own copy of the step at 0xFC88.

0xfc88.name: read the second protection word, then step the two-bit counter
0xfc88.why: `tst.w $1461bc` - the other board ROM window - then the same `addq.w #$1,d0; andi.w #$3,d0; move.b d0,$3e0de2` tail as 0xFC32 reaches through 0xFC3A.

0x11bd8.name: cell address
0x11bd8.why: byte at 4(a7) shifted left five, plus the byte at 5(a7), plus 0x3e0864 - the board base, 32 bytes to a row. It is the exact inverse of the decomposition 0x5e38 does to turn a cell address back into a coordinate pair.

0x11bec.name: screen address
0x11bec.why: byte at 5(a7) shifted left nine, plus the byte at 4(a7), all shifted left three, plus 0x200004. That is (y * 512 + x) * 8: 0x200 is the playfield row stride 0x5892 copies with and 0x200004 its base, so a cell is eight pixels across and a row of cells is eight screen rows.

0x11c04.name: follow the header's self-relative pointer and copy from there
0x11c04.why: `move.w (a0),d0; adda.l d0,a0` - the first word of the block is an offset to itself, which is how this ROM's graphics headers point at their own data - and then copies from the address that yields.

0x11cf8.name: aiming direction
0x11cf8.why: takes the two word arguments as a dx and a dy, works with their absolute values, and picks one of three positions within a quadrant by comparing 16 times one against 7 times the other - a ratio of 7:16, which is 0.4375 where the exact octant boundary tan 22.5 degrees is 0.4142. Mostly-vertical gives 2, mostly-horizontal 0, diagonal 1. It then folds the signs back in: a negative dx negates and adds 4, a negative dy negates and adds 8, and the result is masked to 7. Eight directions, which is the space the cannon aiming at 0x6c20 steps around with the same mask.

0x11d5c.name: distance
0x11d5c.why: an approximate hypotenuse. It takes the absolute values of the two word arguments, swaps them so the larger is in d0, forms the smaller squared divided by the larger, and answers larger + that/2 - that/8 - which is max + three eighths of min squared over max. The bvc after the divu substitutes 0x7fff when it overflows, and a zero pair returns zero without dividing.

0x11d96.name: scaling blitter
0x11d96.why: stretches the rectangle 0x5892 grabbed into 0x21e000 as it copies it out. Both axes run on the same accumulator trick: a counter starts at 0x40 and the scale step is subtracted from it, and while it stays positive the same source byte is written again or the whole row just written is copied again. Rows advance by 0x200, the playfield stride. So the ratio is 64 to the step the caller passes.

0x11e10.name: screen dissolve
0x11e10.why: waits for the frame at 0x512, clears 0x3c0000, then walks 0xf000 offsets of the playfield at 0x200004 in the order of a maximal-length shift register - x >>= 1 with an eor of 0xb400 when a 1 falls off, retried until the value is back below 0xf000 - clearing a word at each. Every offset once, in an order that looks random, which is what makes it a dissolve rather than a wipe. It ends with a jmp to 0x52a rather than an rts.

0x11e58.name: RNG
0x11e58.why: a 16-bit linear congruential generator whose state is the word at 0x3e0842: x = x * 0x3619 + 0x5d35. The new state is then multiplied by the caller's longword argument and the high half taken - swap and ext.l - which scales the result into the range the caller asked for rather than masking it.

0x11eda.name: decompress the graphics at 0xE5930
0x11eda.why: `movem.l d1-d4/a0-a1,-(a7); lea $e5930.l,a0; bra.b $11f08` - the same shared body as 0x11EE6 and 0x11EF2, pointed at a third fixed source.

0x11ee6.name: decompress the graphics at 0xf1d8a
0x11ee6.why: `movem.l d1-d4/a0-a1,-(a7); lea $f1d8a.l,a0; bra.b $11f08` - saves, points a0 at one fixed source, and joins the shared body at 0x11f08 that calls the decompressor. The source address is the whole difference between this and 0x11ef2.

0x11ef2.name: decompress the graphics at 0xdaddc
0x11ef2.why: `movem.l d1-d4/a0-a1,-(a7); lea $daddc.l,a0; bra.b $11f08` - the same shared body as 0x11ee6, pointed at a different fixed source.

0x11f2a.name: graphics decompressor
0x11f2a.why: a run-length decoder for 4-bit pixels. Every path writes bytes to (a1)+ and wraps the destination the same way - dbra on a counter of 7, then adda 0x1f8 and reload 7 - which is an eight-byte-wide column on a 0x200 row stride, so 0x1f8 is the stride less the width. d2 is added to every pixel, which is the palette base. A positive control byte carries its own count in the high nibble and its pixel in the low one. A negative one takes its count from the low five bits and the next two bits pick the form: skip that many, two pixels packed in one following byte, one following byte repeated, or two following bytes alternated. 0xfc is the terminator, and it is the only way out.

0x11ff8.name: block recolour
0x11ff8.why: walks an eight by eight block - dbra from 7 twice, with adda 0x1f8 between rows, the same geometry the decompressor at 0x11f2a writes - and rewrites each byte as its low nibble plus the word argument. So it moves a block from one palette bank to another and touches nothing else about it.

0x120a2.name: decode a run-length stream, three opcode shapes
0x120a2.why: a non-negative byte is a literal run; a negative one keeps its low five bits as a count and the next two bits, shifted out with `asl.b`, choose between a repeated byte, a two-byte pattern and a back-reference.

0x1217e.name: rect palette remap
0x1217e.why: rewrites a rectangle of pixels through a sixteen-entry table. For each byte the HIGH nibble indexes the table at 0x18(a7) and the entry is added to the LOW nibble, so the top half selects which remap applies and the bottom half is the pixel. Width and height come from 0x1c and 0x20(a7), and between rows it takes the width back off the pointer and adds 0x200, the playfield stride.

0x121c4.name: decode one eight-by-eight block from two sources into the playfield
0x121c4.why: points a0 and a3 into the graphics at 0xDADDC by two separate word offsets, runs decompressorInnerLoop and rleDecoderVariant for each of eight columns, stepping the destination one byte at a time and 0x1F8 at the end of a row, and returns the destination advanced by eight.

0x122ae.name: store the byte in d0 through a1

0x12306.name: start a decoder run with the emit table at 0x12354
0x12306.why: `lea $12354.l,a4` - the pair of emit helpers - then reads two bytes through a3, biases each by a5, doubles d5 and sets its low bit, and joins the decoder body at 0x1232A.

0x124be.name: terrain painter
0x124be.why: sets up the eight-wide, 0x200-stride geometry the block routines all share - d4 counts 8 then becomes 7, d5 is 0x200 minus 8, which is the 0x1f8 wrap - and branches to the worker at 0x124e2 with the source at 0x20(a7) and the destination at 0x24(a7). It answers a0, the source pointer the worker left behind, so a caller can paint one block after another from a single stream.

0x12574.name: emit two decoded bytes a row at a time
0x12574.why: `move.b (a0)+,d0; move.b (a0)+,d3` then each written through a1 with a `dbra` on the row counter, and at the end of a row `adda.l d5,a1` and the counter reloaded to 0x1FF less the stride. The two-byte inner loop of the decoder at 0x124E4.

0x1262a.name: the palette RAM operations, one entry each
0x1262a.why: every entry addresses the palette with `movep.w`, which is what makes this routine palette-specific: the RAM is byte-wide on a sixteen-bit bus, so a colour is two bytes four apart. The first entry adds four separate deltas to the intensity bit and the three five-bit channels, masking each back into place with 0x8000, 0x7C00, 0x3E0 and 0x1F; the others rotate a run of entries forwards or backwards by the count at +0xF. All of them leave through 0x12880.

0x1288e.name: return immediately
0x1288e.why: `rts` at the head, and what capstone shows after it is data: this address is a routine only because something calls it, and calling it does nothing. Named for the instruction that is really there rather than for the sixteen bytes the extent covers.

0x13000.name: clear the playfield and work RAM, kicking the watchdog
0x13000.why: two `clr.w (a0)+` loops with `dbeq` - 0x200000 to 0x21FFFE and 0x3E0000 to 0x3E07FE - each restarting with a write to the watchdog at 0x72FFFE so the board does not reset while the clear runs.

0x130f8.name: run the two self-test passes and return the second's result
0x130f8.why: `bsr.w $13662` then `bsr.w $136ee`, and `move.l d5,d0` for the answer, with every register saved around them. 0x1310C below it is a separate entry: it clears the playfield up to 0x3E07FE, kicks the watchdog at 0x72FFFE on each pass, and jumps to 0x300 when it finishes.

0x13134.name: self test failure report
0x13134.why: takes a record through a0: a word that goes to 0x72fffe - the watchdog port the whole self test pokes to stay alive - then a byte pair written into 0x3c0000 at a stride of 4 for 0x101 entries, then a second word and a second pair written into 0x3c0018 at a stride of 0x10 for nine more. It returns with jmp (a4), not rts, which is the self test's own convention: a4 holds where to go next and a6 holds the step after that, because this code runs before there is a usable stack.

0x133a6.name: mask interrupts and restart through the reset vector
0x133a6.why: `move.w #$2700,sr; suba.l a0,a0; movea.l (a0)+,a7; movea.l (a0),a0; jmp (a0)` - zeroes a0, loads the stack pointer and entry address from the first eight bytes of the image, and jumps. That is a reset.

0x13408.name: read both input ports and step the self-test cursor
0x13408.why: packs 0x640000 and 0x640002 into one long, inverts it - the ports are active low - and masks off the bits that are not buttons, then steps the cursor at 0x3E368B by 5 or 4 depending on its sign.

0x1357c.name: power on self test
0x1357c.why: the entry the board comes up on. It masks all interrupts with sr = 0x2700, points a7 at 0x3e32fe, fills 0x3c0000 to 0x3c07fc with an incrementing word and kicks 0x72fffe in a loop. It then walks a table at 0x1325e in 14-byte entries - lea -$e(a5) steps back over one - each holding a flag long, a start and end pointer, and a word choosing between the RAM test at 0x1378e and 0x1397a. A failure is reported through 0x13134 and then the switches at 0x640000 decide what happens: bit 0 holds the failure on screen, bit 3 advances. When the table runs out it calls 0x13000 and jumps to 0x13350.

0x13662.name: checksum every ROM region against its stored sum
0x13662.why: walks the region table at 0x132F8 as start/end pairs, sums each, and compares against the answers at 0x13328, kicking the watchdog and recording the result in 0x3E3D7A and 0x3E3D7B.

0x136ee.name: checksum every ROM region, reporting the address of the first bad one
0x136ee.why: the same region table at 0x132F8, but this one keeps the region's base shifted into the high word so a failure names where it was.

0x1378e.name: ram test all patterns
0x1378e.why: the RAM test, run as a chain of steps rather than as calls: a6 holds the next step and a4 the failure exit, and every step ends jmp (a6) or jmp (a4), because there is no stack yet. a3 is 0x72fffe and is written inside every inner loop so the watchdog cannot trip during a long pass. The steps are a fill with d0, a walking-bit pass upward from 0x8000 and the same pass with the complement (d5 = 0 or 0xff), then a walking-bit pass downward from the top of the region, with 0xff and 0x00 fills between them. Each pass reads before it writes and leaves the eor of expected against actual in d0 on the way out, so the failure exit gets the bits that differed.

0x1380e.name: ram test fill with pattern
0x1380e.why: one step of the chain at 0x1378e, which is why facts.json has no extent for it - it is a label inside that routine, entered by a branch with a6 already loaded. lea -$2(a1),a0 then addq.w #$2,a0 before each write walks the region from a1 up to a2 writing the word in d0, with move.w d0,(a3) after every one so the watchdog at 0x72fffe cannot trip during a long region, and it leaves through jmp (a6) rather than rts.

0x1381e.name: ram test walking bit up
0x1381e.why: the walking-bit pass upward, and the two entry points 0x1381e and 0x13822 differ only in the background: clr.l d5 for zeroes, moveq #$ff,d5 for ones. d7 starts at 0x8000 and lsr.w #$1 walks the bit down through the word while the address stays put, reading and comparing against the expected value BEFORE each write, so a cell that does not hold what was last written is caught the moment the next bit is tried. A mismatch leaves the eor of expected against actual in d0 and takes jmp (a4), the failure exit; a clean pass walks the region back down comparing again and continues at a6.

0x13864.name: ram test walking bit down
0x13864.why: the same pass in the other direction, and the same pair of entries for the two backgrounds - clr.l d5 and moveq #$ff,d5. It starts at the top with lea $2(a2),a0 and subq.w #$2,a0, and the bit walks the other way too: d7 is 1 and lsl.w #$1 carries it up through the word. Running the region downward with the bit ascending catches address-line faults the ascending pass at 0x1381e cannot, which is why both are in the chain.

0x1397a.name: the RAM test's pass sequence, chained through a6
0x1397a.why: eleven passes over the region a1..a2, each written as `lea $X(pc),a6; bra <pass>` so the pass returns with `jmp (a6)` to the address after it - a continuation chain rather than calls, which is why the routine has eleven entry points. The passes are a fill, two walking-bit sweeps, and their inverses with d0 = 0xFF; the watchdog at 0x72FFFE is kicked throughout, and bit 3 of 0x640002 skips the second half.

0x13b8c.name: write the four sound registers for a channel
0x13b8c.why: two calls to bitfieldExtract - register 4 then 0x17, taking the longs the caller points at and the byte at 0x3E3D7B - then two to soundCallThreeLongArgs, registers 0xD and 0x21. Every register number is an immediate.

0x13c36.name: write the self-test result into the sound registers
0x13c36.why: steps the counter at 0x3E3D7B, and calls bitfieldExtract with 1 and that counter and the string at 0x13CC6.

0x13d1a.name: return one
0x13d1a.why: `moveq #$1,d0; rts`. A constant-true result for a caller that tests d0.

0x13e0a.name: format a time as hours, minutes and seconds separated by colons
0x13e0a.why: divides by 0xE10 - 3,600 - and formats the quotient, writes 0x3A, divides the remainder by 0x3C and formats that, writes another 0x3A, and formats what is left. Three calls to formatNumberPaddingSeparators at width 2 into consecutive positions.

0x13f98.name: tempo divisor from the sound rate word
0x13f98.why: `tst.b $3e344a` and return -1 if the driver is not running; bit 15 of the rate word at 0x3E3444 set returns 0; otherwise ((0x3E3444 >> 11) & 7) + 1. A divisor between 1 and 8, and the value every routine in this block divides its tick accumulator by. It was `soundEnableCheckVariant`, named for the `tst.b` at its head, which is the guard rather than the answer.

0x13fce.name: advance the tick accumulator and scale it to twelfths
0x13fce.why: carries the fractional ticks at 0x3E3446 into the whole ticks at 0x3E3448 a divisor at a time, clamps the whole count at 30, and returns (whole * 12) / divisor. The divisor is 0x13F98's. Returns -1 when the driver is stopped and 0x18 when the divisor is zero.

0x14044.name: advance the tick accumulator and pack whole, numerator and denominator
0x14044.why: the same carry and clamp as 0x13FCE, then splits the accumulator into whole = acc / divisor and a fraction acc mod divisor over the divisor, halves both until one is odd - lowest terms - special-cases 3/6 to 1/2, and returns whole in the high word, numerator in bits 8-15 and denominator in the low byte.

0x14138.name: take a count of ticks from the accumulator if there are that many
